title: How Does a State ID Get Into Apple Wallet and Google Wallet?
summary: Adding a mobile driver’s license to your phone may take seconds, but behind that simple tap is a chain of verification, cryptography, and trust decisions that make the credential usable.
body_markdown:
A resident opens the wallet app, taps “add ID,” photographs their license, and a few moments later a digital version of their driver’s license sits next to their payment cards. It looks simple. Underneath, that single tap sets off issuance, cryptographic signing, and a trust chain that lets a card reader confirm the ID is genuine without calling the DMV. Here is how each step works, and the governance choices a state makes before any of it is possible.


A driver’s license in a platform wallet is a form of verifiable digital credential: data signed by an issuer so anyone can check that it is authentic and unaltered.


## How your license gets into the wallet


Issuance begins at the DMV, not with Apple or Google. When you add a license, the wallet app captures the front and back of your physical card and a short selfie video, then submits them to your state’s issuing agency for verification.[Google’s own instructions](https://support.google.com/wallet/answer/12436402?ref=blog.spruceid.com) describe this photograph-and-video step and note that the submission is verified with the government agency that issued your ID.


Once the DMV confirms the match, it issues a cryptographically signed mobile driver’s license (an[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) credential) and provisions it to secure hardware on your device. The state remains the issuer; the platform provides the wallet that holds the credential. The same authority that grants the physical card signs the digital one, and that shared authority is a large part of what makes the credential trustworthy.


## How you present it, in person and online


In person, your phone and the verifier’s reader connect directly.[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://blog.spruceid.com/how-does-a-state-id-get-into-apple-wallet-and-google-wallet/%E2%80%9Dhttps://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html%E2%80%9D) defines “device engagement”: the reader scans a QR code or taps over NFC, then exchanges data over that short-range link, which can include Bluetooth. At participating TSA checkpoints, both Apple and Google IDs are read this way, using NFC or a QR code.


Online presentment uses a companion specification,[ISO/IEC TS 18013-7](https://www.iso.org/standard/91154.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , which extends the same mDL to web and app transactions over the internet. The credential and its protections can travel with you, whether you are at an airport counter or a website age gate.


## How a verifier knows the ID is real


Verifiers generally trust an mDL through issuer certificates rather than a live database lookup. Each state DMV signs its credentials with keys anchored to a root certificate. The American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA) runs a[Digital Trust Service](https://www.aamva.org/identity/mobile-driver-license-digital-trust-service?ref=blog.spruceid.com) that gives relying parties a single, secure way to obtain the verified public keys of each issuing authority.


A verifier loads those keys into its reader in advance. When your phone presents an mDL, the reader checks the signature against the known issuer keys and confirms the credential came from a legitimate DMV and has not been altered. Because trust can live in the certificates, verification can work offline, and the DMV is not told that a check happened.


## What privacy should you expect?


A well-built mDL shares only what is asked, and the design aims to keep your usage private. Three properties matter:


1. **Selective disclosure:** A reader can request a specific subset of fields, for example, proof you are over 21, or just your photo and name, and the wallet responds with only that subset.[Apple states](https://support.apple.com/en-us/118260?ref=blog.spruceid.com) that its ID responds with the requested data only.2. **Reader authentication and consent:** You see what is being requested and approve it with Face ID, Touch ID, or a device lock before anything is shared.3. **No issuer surveillance:**[Apple states](https://support.apple.com/en-us/118260?ref=blog.spruceid.com) that neither Apple nor the issuing state can see when or where you present your ID. Google offers an optional activity history, turned off by default, that only you can view on your device.


These are among the properties that distinguish a verifiable digital credential from a physical ID card: you prove a fact without handing over everything, and no one logs your movements.


## Platform wallets versus state-endorsed and open wallets


The two approaches involve real tradeoffs. Platform wallets are already on most residents’ phones and require no additional download, but they give the platform significant control over enrollment terms, user experience, and feature roadmap. State-operated or third-party wallets give the state direct governance over policy, user experience, and data handling, but require residents to install a separate app. Both approaches use the same ISO/IEC 18013-5 and 18013-7 mDL standards underneath.


The choice is not binary. A state’s issuance infrastructure can issue credentials to both platform wallets (Apple Wallet, Google Wallet) and state-operated or third-party wallets simultaneously. California’s mDL program, which[SpruceID built in partnership with the California DMV](https://spruceid.com/success-stories/california-dmv-mobile-driver-license?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , takes exactly this approach: the same issuance backend provisions credentials to the state’s own open-source wallet app and to platform wallets, giving residents the choice of where to hold their credential while giving the state control over the issuance and trust infrastructure.


This dual-path model means states do not have to pick one approach at launch and live with it. The right strategy depends on the state’s priorities: maximizing immediate reach (platform wallets are already installed), maintaining governance control (state-operated wallets), or both. The tradeoffs are real, and the best answer varies by state context, resident demographics, and policy goals. A few common misconceptions about these choices are worth clearing up before a program launches, and we address several in[Debunking Myths about the Mobile Driver’s License](https://blog.spruceid.com/debunking-myths-about-the-mobile-drivers-license-2/) .


## What residents and program owners should look for


**Residents:** check whether your state appears on Apple’s or Google’s official supported list before expecting the feature. The lists differ by platform and change over time. Keep your physical card; Google notes that a digital ID is not a replacement for your physical ID.


**Program owners:** favor[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) and[18013-7](https://www.iso.org/standard/91154.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) conformance, AAMVA trust-service participation, selective disclosure, and a no-phone-home design. Those choices help keep your wallet interoperable and your residents’ movements private, regardless of which wallet holds the card.
